textbookText: Transverse binary fission This type of reproduction takes place during favourable condition at the availability of food, suitable temperature etc. Paramecium caudatum divides 2-3 times a day by this process. Entire process completes in about 1-2 hours. In transverse binary fission, Paramecium divides in such a way that plane of division is right angle to the axis of the body. In this process, division of nucleus (karyokinesis) is followed by the division of cytoplasm (cytokinesis). Following events occur for the completion of transverse binary fission:

Figure 8.1.11 Transverse binary fission in Paramecium i. Paramecium stops feeding and its oral groove or buccal structure also disappears. ii. At that time, micronucleus divides by mitosis to form two daughter nuclei and each move towards the opposite end. iii. Simultaneously, macronucleus becomes elongated and constricted at the middle to divide by amitosis. Daughter macronuclei also move to the opposite pole. iv. Now, two oral grooves start to form, one at the anterior half and another at the posterior half on the ventral side. v. Each half develops a new contractile vacuole at the required position. Buccal structures also start to reappear. vi. Meanwhile, a transverse constriction or furrow appears at the middle region which deepens and finally cytoplasm is also divided to form two daughter Paramecia. vii. Anterior daughter Paramecium is called proter and posterior one is called opisthe. Daughter Paramecia produced by this process are called clone because they are genetically similar. After many generations, the rate of binary fission becomes slow and may stops. So, they should be rejuvenated frequently by conjugation.

Conjugation It is the simplest method of sexual reproduction in which temporary union of two Paramecia of same species but different strain takes place to exchange their genetic materials. It is a significant process that should occur frequently between transverse binary fissions because after many generations (about 300 asexual generations), Paramecium is unable to reproduce Biology, Grade 11 | 296

asexually. Paramecia undergoing conjugation are morphologically similar but physiologically different, called pre-conjugants. Factors which induce conjugation are: i. Insufficient supply of food or starvation. ii. Being genetically and physiologically weak and small due to continued binary fission. iii. Sudden darkness or fall in temperature in some species. iv. A specific protein present in cilia of mating individual.

Events that occur in conjugation 1. Two Paramecium caudatum of different strain or mating type come in contact ventrally and unite by their oral grooves. 2. Buccal structures disappear and feeding is also stopped. 3. At the point of contact, pellicle and ectoplasm also dissolve forming protoplasmic bridge between them and Paramecia at this moment are called conjugants. 4. The macronucleus degenerates into pieces and absorbed by cytoplasm. Meanwhile, micronucleus grows first and divides by meiosis to yield four haploid daughter micronuclei. 5. Out of four daughter micronuclei, three get degenerated and remaining one divides by mitosis to produce two unequal sized pronuclei or gametic nuclei. 6. Among two pronuclei, smaller sized and active nucleus behaves as migratory or male gametic nucleus whereas larger sized and passive nucleus behaves as stationary or female gametic nucleus. 7. Each migratory or male gametic nucleus moves from one conjugant to another through protoplasmic bridge and fuses with stationary or female gametic nucleus. 8. Now, zygote nucleus or synkaryon is formed. This phenomenon of complete fusion of two nuclei from different individual is also called amphimixis. 9. After 12- 48 hours of union of two individuals, they become separated and now called ex-conjugants. 10. In each ex-conjugant, zygote nucleus divides thrice by mitosis to produce eight nuclei. Out of them, four nuclei become enlarged to form macronuclei and remaining four become micronuclei. 11. Among four micronuclei, three micronuclei get degenerated. 12. Now, remaining micronucleus of each ex-conjugant divides mitotically and transverse binary fission in Paramecium occurs to produce two daughter Paramecia, each with two macronuclei and one micronucleus. 13. The daughter Paramecium, so produced, again divides by binary fission to produce two Paramecia, each with one micronucleus and one macronucleus. 14. In this way, altogether eight daughter Paramecia are produced at the end which are genetically different.

Figure 8.1.12 Conjugation in Paramecium Significance of conjugation i. Conjugation brings nuclear re-arrangement or re-organization which is essential for the continuation of binary fission. ii. Conjugation is the means of rejuvenation maintaining vitality and genetic vigour in offsprings. iii. It brings about the replacement of macro or meganucleus with the material from zygote nucleus.
